Writing the adjacency matrix in block form with respect to $S$ and $\bar S$ gives $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&B\\B^T&C\end{pmatrix}$, since $S$ is independent. I take $q = \dfrac{x_{\bar S}^T C\, x_{\bar S}}{x_{\bar S}^T x_{\bar S}}$, the Rayleigh quotient of $A[\bar S]$ at $x_{\bar S}$. Let $s=\sum_{v\in S}x_v^2$, so $\|x_{\bar S}\|^2 = 1-s$.

The eigenvalue equations $Ax=\lambda x$ split into two blocks:
- $B x_{\bar S}=\lambda x_S$
- $B^T x_S + C x_{\bar S}=\lambda x_{\bar S}$

Multiply the second equation on the left by $x_{\bar S}^T$. Using the first equation, $x_{\bar S}^T B^T x_S = x_S^T B x_{\bar S} = \lambda s$, so
$$\lambda s + q(1-s)=\lambda(1-s).$$

Solving for $s$ gives $s=\dfrac{\lambda-q}{2\lambda-q}$. Therefore
$$\frac12-s=\frac{(2\lambda-q)-2(\lambda-q)}{2(2\lambda-q)}=\frac{q}{2(2\lambda-q)}=\frac{q}{4\lambda-2q}.$$

Check on $K_3$ with $S=\{1\}$: $\lambda=2$ and $q=1$, so the formula gives $1/6$. The direct value is $1/2-1/3=1/6$, which agrees.

Now compare the three solutions:
- Solution 1 answers $\tfrac12-\tfrac{q}{2\lambda}$, which gives $0$ on $K_3$ instead of $1/6$.
- Solution 2 answers $q-\tfrac12$, which is not the derived value.
- Solution 3 answers $q$, which is not the derived value.

None matches $\dfrac{q}{2(2\lambda-q)}$.

CHOICE: NONE
